lucy: quick heads up — saw a host-side CPU spike on prod ingest nodes ~10:12UTC. p99 full-request latency climbed from ~120ms -> ~350ms, overall host CPU from 15% -> 40% on the acceptor hostpool. attaching flamegraph and a short perf snippet :eyes:

lucy: https://perf.corp/redwood/flame/8532107777 (flame + collapsed)

raj: looking — flame shows huge tail in `acceptor::handle_read` and kernel syscalls `writev` + `epoll_wait` in a tight loop. interestingly most of the time is in small writes (100-800B) from the streaming framing layer.

raj: `perf top` excerpt:
```
  27.4%  host_acceptor  [.] acceptor::handle_read
  18.1%  libc.so        [.] writev
  12.3%  kernel         [.] __epoll_wait
   8.7%  host_parse     [.] tokenize
```

ashley: did we roll any batching heuristic or acceptor change recently? I remember a PR that tried to prioritize low-latency tiny writes for streaming.

lucy: yes — PR #8423 changed acceptor batching to flush immediately if the message seemed latency-sensitive (small token deltas). the intent was good but under high concurrency it prevents coalescing and forces many writev syscalls. kvcache hit rates stayed stable, kv behavior not the culprit.

devin: marker — this matches the incident from the perf-regen test yesterday where the host-side overhead dominated. streaming chunking produced many <1KB frames and the kernel got saturated.

lucy: measured numbers from canary x3:
- baseline (old heuristic): host CPU 14-18%, p99 115ms
- canary (new heuristic): host CPU 38-42%, p99 330-370ms
- writev syscalls per sec x4

raj: two levers to try: 1) coalesce at acceptor for up to N ms (micro-coalesce) so we batch small writes into a single writev, 2) change kernel socket buffer / TCP corking hints so writev fewer syscalls. both are cheap to toggle.

ashley: agree. also consider making the batching decision aware of current CPU/epoll backlog — the heuristic can dynamically fall back to batch when syscalls/sec > threshold. that keeps tail low and preserves latency for low load.

lucy: quick patch I'm validating locally: add `--acceptor-coalesce-ms=1` default 0, and a dynamic path that checks `syscalls/sec > 1000` to force coalesce. small patch + unit tests. I'll push a canary PR (WIP) 

lucy: snippet:
```
if (config.coalesce_ms > 0 || syscalls_per_sec > COALESCE_THRESHOLD) {
  buffer.append(msg);
  if (buffer.size() >= WRITEV_BATCH_BYTES || now - last_flush >= coalesce_ms) flush();
} else {
  flush(msg);
}
```

devin: also check the kernel `tcp_quickack` and `tcp_cork` behavior on our distro — quick wins there. I can run a small host-level experiment to compare writev counts with `tcp_cork` on vs off.

lucy: thanks. I'll open the canary PR: https://git.corp/redwood/acceptor/compare/try-coalesce-8532 (draft). plan: rollback canary, apply patch with `--acceptor-coalesce-ms=1`, measure for 15m, then toggle dynamic path.

infra-bot: Canary rollback executed for cluster acceptor-prod-3 at 10:40UTC (reason: latency regression) :warning:

ashley: sounds good. if the dynamic heuristic is low-risk we can opt it into canary immediately. devin, want to collect the syscalls/sec counters for the last 2 hours from node-exporter?

devin: on it. will post graphs in ~10m.

lucy: opened PR and added test coverage for coalescing and a small perf microbenchmark. tagging @raj @ashley for review.

raj: quick nit on the patch — prefer using `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW)` for interval calc to avoid jumps. otherwise :thumbsup:.

ashley: approving once we have devin's syscall numbers. :+1:

lucy: thanks all. goal: reduce writev syscalls by ~3x and get p99 back under 150ms without hurting tail for low-load. will update after canary run. :thinking:
